in_approved_education.description: Whether the child is in approved education or training (e.g. A-levels, GCSEs, NVQ up to level 3). Only relevant for children aged 16-19.

another_claimant_has_priority.description: Whether another person who also lives with the child has priority for claiming Child Benefit.

another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

test_case.agent_script:
=== YOUR SITUATION PROFILE ===
You live in the UK.
You are inquiring about your 1 child:
  - Alex is 8 years old and lives with you.

Here are the exact details of your circumstances to use when answering the agent's questions:

Regarding Alex:
  - Claimant lives in the UK
  - Child is 8 (under 16)
  - Child lives with claimant
  - Child is not in local authority care
  - Child in hospital for 15 weeks but claimant regularly spends on child
  - Child is not fostered
  - Child does not work 24+ hours/week
  - Child has not started an apprenticeship in England
  - Child does not receive qualifying benefits in their own right

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: I'll help you determine if you're eligible for Child Benefit. Let me start by getting the first question in the assessment process.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! To get started, I need to know about your child or children.

**How old is the child or children you're claiming for?**

Please tell me:
1. **How many children** are you claiming for?
2. **Their ages** (or date of birth)

This information will help me determine which path to follow in the eligibility assessment. 

The basic rule is:
- **Under 16**: Generally qualify for Child Benefit
- **16-19**: May qualify if they're in education or approved training
- **20 or older**: Do not qualify

Please provide these details so I can continue with your assessment.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Hi, thanks for helping me with this. I'm looking to claim for my son Alex. He's 8 years old and lives with me at home.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Perfect, thank you for that information! So you're claiming for **Alex, who is 8 years old**. Since Alex is under 16, he's in the automatic qualification category. Let me move to the next check.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Excellent! Now I need to check the following:

**Is Alex working less than 24 hours per week, or is he not in any paid work at all?**

Since Alex is 8 years old, I expect the answer is that he's not in paid work, but I need to confirm this for the assessment.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, he's not working at all - he's only 8, so he's just at primary school.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Perfect! That's exactly what I expected. So Alex is not in any paid work - he's just at primary school. Let me continue with the next check.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now I need to check:

**Is Alex NOT receiving certain benefits in their own right, such as Employment and Support Allowance (ESA) or Universal Credit?**

Again, given Alex's age, I'd expect he's not receiving these benefits, but I need to confirm this for the assessment.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: That's right, he doesn't receive any benefits in his own name. He's just a kid.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Great! That confirms Alex doesn't receive any benefits in his own name. Let me move to the next check.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now I need to check about apprenticeships:

**Is Alex NOT in an apprenticeship, or if he is, is it an approved one?**

Given that Alex is 8 years old and at primary school, I expect he's not in any apprenticeship. Can you confirm this?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, he's definitely not in an apprenticeship - he's far too young for that. He's just in primary school.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Perfect! That's what I expected. Alex is clearly not in any apprenticeship. Let me continue to the next stage of the assessment.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now I need to check your residency status, as this is an important requirement for Child Benefit eligibility.

**Where do you normally live?**

There are several paths that could make you eligible:

1. **Normally live in the UK** - the most straightforward
2. **Have settled status** under the EU Settlement Scheme
3. **Have pre-settled status** under the EU Settlement Scheme (with additional requirements like working, studying, or having sufficient resources)
4. **Crown servant** living abroad in certain qualifying countries

Which of these applies to your situation? Or do you normally live in the UK?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: I live in the UK - I'm in Manchester with Alex.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Excellent! You live in the UK in Manchester with Alex. That means you meet the residency requirement. Let me proceed to the next check.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now I need to confirm:

**Are you responsible for Alex?**

Based on what you've already told me, you live with Alex at home, which means you definitely meet this requirement. But let me confirm for the assessment:

Do you live with Alex and support his upkeep (food, clothes, housing, etc.)?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, absolutely - he lives with me at home and I take care of all his needs.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Perfect! You live with Alex and you're responsible for his care and upkeep. That clearly satisfies this requirement. Let me continue.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now I need to check an important point:

**Is anyone else claiming Child Benefit for Alex, or has anyone else applied for it?**

This is important because only one person can claim Child Benefit for each child. So:
- Is Alex's mother/father or any other person also claiming or trying to claim for Alex?
- Or are you the only person claiming for him?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, nobody else is claiming Child Benefit for Alex. I'm the only one claiming for him.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Great! You're the only person claiming for Alex. Let me continue with the next check.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now I need to check Alex's living situation:

**Where is Alex currently living?**

- Is he living normally at home with you in Manchester?
- Or is he in hospital, care (such as a children's home or residential institution), or being fostered?

Given what you've already told me, I expect he's living normally with you at home, but I need to confirm this.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Well, actually, Alex has been in hospital for a while now - a few months. But I still visit him regularly and buy things for him like clothes, magazines, and his favorite snacks.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for clarifying that. I understand Alex is currently in hospital and you're still actively supporting him. This is an important detail that affects the eligibility check.

Let me proceed to the next question:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
This is an important check. I need to understand the duration of Alex's hospital stay:

**How long has Alex been in hospital in total?**

Important details:
- Has Alex been in hospital continuously for a few months?
- Or has he had multiple stays? (If so, when did each stay begin and end?)
- Have there been any breaks of 28 days or more between hospital stays?

The rule is that Child Benefit can continue for up to 12 weeks (84 days) in hospital. If there are multiple stays with less than 28 days between them, they're added together. But if there are 28+ days between stays, the counter resets.

You mentioned "a few months" - can you be more specific about exactly how long he's been in hospital?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: He's been there for about 15 weeks now, continuously. It's been quite a long stay unfortunately.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I'm sorry to hear Alex has had such a long hospital stay. That's 15 weeks continuously, which exceeds the 12-week limit for Child Benefit eligibility during hospital stays.

However, let me check the next criterion, which is about your regular spending on Alex while he's in hospital:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Perfect! There's an important exception to the 12-week rule:

**Are you regularly spending money on Alex while he's in hospital?**

You mentioned you visit him regularly and buy things for him like clothes, magazines, and snacks. This could qualify as "regularly spending money" on him, which would be an exception to the 12-week limit.

Can you confirm: Are you regularly spending your own money on Alex (like the clothes, magazines, snacks you mentioned) while he's in the hospital?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, definitely - I'm regularly spending money on him. I buy his clothes, magazines, and his favorite foods to bring when I visit.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Excellent! You're regularly spending money on Alex while he's in hospital - this is an important exception to the 12-week rule. Let me continue with the assessment.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now for the final check:

**Is the local council NOT paying towards Alex's hospital accommodation or maintenance?**

In other words:
- Is the hospital care being fully funded by the NHS (National Health Service)?
- Or is the local council contributing towards his care or maintenance costs?

This is important because if the council is paying for his care, you wouldn't be eligible for Child Benefit.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, the council isn't paying anything - it's just NHS hospital care.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Perfect! The NHS is covering Alex's hospital care, and the local council is not paying towards his accommodation or maintenance. This means you've met all the eligibility requirements.

Let me proceed to the final outcome:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Excellent news! Now let me report your eligibility outcome:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
## ✅ **You are ELIGIBLE for Child Benefit for Alex**

### Summary of Your Eligibility:

**Positive factors:**
- ✅ Alex is 8 years old (under 16 - automatic qualification)
- ✅ He is not working full-time
- ✅ He is not receiving benefits in his own right
- ✅ He is not in any disqualifying apprenticeship
- ✅ You live in the UK (Manchester)
- ✅ You live with Alex and are responsible for his care
- ✅ You are the only person claiming for him
- ✅ You regularly spend money on Alex while in hospital (clothes, magazines, snacks)
- ✅ The NHS is funding his hospital care (not the local council)

**Important exception applied:** Although Alex has been in hospital for 15 weeks (which exceeds the normal 12-week limit), your regular spending on him qualifies as an important exception to this time limit. This means Child Benefit can continue.

### Next Steps:

1. **Apply for Child Benefit** online or by post using form CH2
2. **Provide required documents:**
   - Proof of your identity
   - Alex's birth certificate or adoption certificate
3. **Important note about High Income Child Benefit Charge:** If you or your partner earns over £60,000 per year, you may be subject to the High Income Child Benefit Charge (which means you may have to repay some or all of the benefit). Check the government website for details.
4. **Payment frequency:** Child Benefit is paid every 4 weeks (or weekly if you're a single parent or receiving certain benefits)

### Helpful Links:
- https://www.gov.uk/child-benefit/how-to-claim
- https://www.gov.uk/child-benefit-for-children-in-hospital-or-care

Congratulations, and I hope Alex makes a good recovery soon! 🎉

reasonings: Alex is eligible for Child Benefit because: (1) He is 8 years old (under 16, automatic qualification); (2) He is not working full-time; (3) He is not receiving benefits in his own right (ESA or Universal Credit); (4) He is not in a disqualifying apprenticeship; (5) You live in the UK (Manchester), meeting residency requirements; (6) You live with Alex and are responsible for his care and upkeep; (7) You are the only person claiming for him; (8) Although Alex has been in hospital for 15 weeks (exceeding the normal 12-week limit), you regularly spend money on him (clothes, magazines, snacks) which qualifies as an exception to the time limit; (9) The local council is not paying towards his hospital care or maintenance - it is NHS-funded.
arguments.overall_reasoning: You are eligible for Child Benefit for Alex. Despite his extended hospital stay of 15 weeks, your regular spending on him while in hospital qualifies as an important exception to the standard 12-week limit. All other eligibility criteria are clearly met, and the NHS funding (not council funding) of his care means there are no barriers to your claim."
